messages.author: 606e45efb8cf41ae
messages.subject: gpagen coding error?
parts:
I've checked this on a couple of datasets now. 

The 'shapes' gpagen$coords produces are not unit size. They vary. The mean of gpagen$coords [apply(gpagen$coords, c(1,2), mean)] is however a configuration of unit size. My guess is that these two things are related within the function. But I think the priorities are backwards. The observations need to be shapes, ie of unit size. The mean configuration maybe doesn't need to be a shape because it is not actually a specimen (i.e., it's not really in the shape space of the observations).

On the other hand, if you take an array of unit size configurations and compute the mean shape with geomorph (mshape), the mean configuration is less than unit size. 

The mshape result makes sense. In my experience, there is always some shrinkage when computing a shape mean. You just live with it because the alternative, where the mean shape is rescaled to unit size, does not allow for mean=0 procrustes residuals.

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] gpagen coding error?
parts:
David,

 

This is not a coding error. The reason for this observation is that in gpagen, the default is Projection=TRUE. That is, following standard GM practice, shapes are aligned using GPA and then projected orthogonally to Tangent Space. This projection results in slight differences in perceived sizes in tangent space (See Rohlf 1999 and others on the relationship of shape space and tangent space and how this is linked through Csize).

 

As a simple example try the following:

 

library(geomorph)

  data(plethodon)

  Y.gpa1 <- gpagen(plethodon$land,PrinAxes=FALSE,Proj=F)

  gpagen(Y.gpa1$coords,Proj=F)$Csize

  Y.gpa2 <- gpagen(plethodon$land,PrinAxes=FALSE,Proj=T)

  gpagen(Y.gpa2$coords,Proj=F)$Csize

 

 

Note that in Y.gpa1, there is no orthogonal projection. In this case the sizes are all equal to 1.0.  However, now your shapes are in the curved hemispherical shape space, making some statistical analyses challenging (ie, those methods that require linear statistics, which is a considerable swath of multivariate statistics).

 

The second example, shapes are aligned and projected into Tangent Space. The sizes vary slightly, but the shapes are in a linear space appropriate for the types of statistics we typically utilize to compare shapes.


Dean
